Beat to Continue Honoring King Crimson on Sprawling 2026 European Tour

[Beat](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/beat), the all-star collective honoring the music of '80s [King Crimson](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/king-crimson), will hit the road again this summer on an extensive European tour.

The supergroup — featuring King Crimson alumni [Adrian Belew](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/adrian-belew) and [Tony Levin](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/tony-levin) plus guitarist [Steve Vai](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/steve-vai/) and [Tool](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/tool) drummer Danny Carey — will launch its tour on June 8 in London. They'll visit Paris, Munich, Prague, Vienna, Barcelona, Istanbul and a myriad of other cities before concluding the run on July 17 in Cmielow, Poland.

"BEAT is coming to Europe in the summer of 2026 to celebrate the incredible 1980s music of King Crimson," Beat and Vai said in a joint [social media statement](https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1Djy3XsaTY/). "It’s going to be a powerful run of shows, and we’d love for you to be part of it. Tickets for most dates are available now—don’t wait, grab yours now!"

**READ MORE:** [The Best Album by Prog's 15 Biggest Artists](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/prog-best-albums/)

Ticketing information can be found at Beat's [website](https://beat-tour.com/?fbclid=IwY2xjawOupWpleHRuA2FlbQIxMABicmlkETFyNnJ6cUljQlRUVTdzaUsyc3J0YwZhcHBfaWQQMjIyMDM5MTc4ODIwMDg5MgABHjAwIADlHHV8fwhRJunrBGPoBFKflyIHuPiYTK1icgnzw3AR_GE3cD-oBk0O_aem_KTJ1DcUds6PDpGCUL4ShOQ). ### Will Beat Record New Music?

News of Beat's 2026 European tour follows the September release of _[Beat Live](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/beat-live-album-release/)_. The album was recorded during a 2024 concert in Los Angeles, and the set list was culled from King Crimson's trio of '80s albums: 1981's _[Discipline](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/king-crimson-discipline-album/)_, 1982's _Beat_ and 1984's _Three of a Perfect Pair_.

![King Crimson - Beat](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0637/9965/6600/files/3910311_550x825.jpg?v=1764101268)

While the band is still focused on playing classic King Crimson songs on the road, Beat hasn't ruled out recording new music.

"Right now, the goal is to honor this King Crimson music the best we can and play anywhere that'll take us," Belew [told UCR](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/king-crimson-beat-new-music/) in early 2025. "But that has a shelf life, obviously. Because once you've toured the world with it, I wouldn't want to go back out and tour the whole world again doing the same thing. Because there's way too many things to do."

## Top 50 Progressive Rock Artists

From Kansas and Can to King Crimson and Curved Air.

Gallery Credit: Ryan Reed

![50. Manfred Manns Earth Band](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-manfred-mann-victor-drees-evening-standard.jpg?w=980&q=75)

50\. Manfred Manns Earth Band

Victor Drees, Getty Images

## 50\. Manfred Mann's Earth Band

They had this spot wrapped up like a douche — oh, wait, wrong lyric. [Manfred Mann](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/manfred-manns-earth-band/)’s career arc is one of the strangest in all of rock: Born and raised in South Africa before moving to the U.K. in the early ‘60s, he started his career as an R&B-rock hitmaker, most famously with breezy covers of “Do Wah Diddy Diddy” and “She La La.” But when his eponymous band split at decade’s end, he pursued a proggier path — first with the experimental jazz-rock outfit Chapter Three, then with the Earth Band. The latter were best known for radically reinventing other people’s songs, including wild versions of [Bruce Springsteen](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/bruce-springsteen/)’s “Blinded by the Light” (a No. 1 U.S. hit) and “Spirit in the Night.” But these covers were more like springboards for their tightly arranged powerhouse performances, particularly their bandleader on organ and synthesizer. The Earth Band released a dozen or so LPs in the solid-to-excellent range — even if they never arrived at one definitive masterpiece. That’s probably why they remain so underrated.

![49. Haken](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-haken_loudwire.jpg?w=980&q=75)

49\. Haken

YouTube / Loudwire

## 49\. Haken

One RateYourMusic user placed Haken on their list of “Non-Masturbatory Progressive Metal” — a worthy categorization for the English sextet. Though every band member is capable of scorching solos, their songs prioritize melody and movement over rote showmanship. Ross Jennings is the key: a frontman equally comfortable with teary-eyed crooning (“The Path”) and expressive belting that could suitably fill a stadium all on its own (“Initiate”). And what a canvas he’s working with! Haken are unpredictable in their sprawl, dabbling in everything from glitchy electronics and ambience to jazz and ‘80s-flavored synth-pop.

![48. Leprous](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-attachment-leprous-trolltoftenes_2021.jpg?w=980&q=75)

48\. Leprous

Troll Toftenes, Leprous

## 48\. Leprous

Too many modern prog-metal bands fall into the traps of overblown djent riffs and empty-calorie virtuosity. But Norway’s Leprous have never been an ordinary prog-metal band, with their meticulous songs built around the operatic voice of Einar Solberg. The frontman’s soaring leads and stacked harmonies blend the grandiosity of vintage metal with the note-perfect technique of [Freddie Mercury](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/freddie-mercury/) and dynamic range of [Jeff Buckley](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/jeff-buckley/) — lofty praise, sure, but he deserves it. The band’s gradual evolution has been fascinating: On albums like 2019’s _Pitfalls_ and 2021’s _Aphelion_, they’ve softened their edges of their sound, with the contact of orchestrations and atmospheric ballads adding more impact to the metallic moments.

![47. Grobschnitt](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-grobschnitt.jpg?w=980&q=75)

47\. Grobschnitt

YouTube

## 47\. Grobschnitt

Grobschnitt are impossible to fully summarize in a one-sentence blurb. But here are some of the highlights: The German group prioritized spaciness and silliness alike — using masks, costumes, weird voices and evocative stage names (Eroc! Mist!) to set them apart from the crowded field. But behind all the superficial quirks, they wrote graceful, melodic symphonic prog that stands up alongside most of the era’s big guns — from the airy swirl of 1977’s _Rockpommel’s Land_ to their expansive, jammy concert opus, 1978’s _Solar Music: Live_.

![46. Strawbs](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-strawbs.jpg?w=980&q=75)

46\. Strawbs

YouTube

## 46\. Strawbs

“Strawbs instinctively play to the songs – the songs are the lifeblood of the band,” Dave Cousins told [It’s Psychedelic Baby](https://www.psychedelicbabymag.com/2021/03/strawbs-dave-cousins-interview.html). “We do not set out to record virtuoso performances over complicated chord sequences, which seems to be the essence of some prog-rock bands.” That methodology makes sense, given that Strawbs began life as a folk act, only blossoming into prog by decorating the margins of their storybook tunes. The true turning point was their fourth LP, 1971’s _From the Witchwood_, featuring a more robust rock attack (including the classically trained keyboard skills of future Yes recruit [Rick Wakeman](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/rick-wakeman/)). And they stayed on fire throughout the decade, crafting one near-masterpiece ( _Grave New World_) after another ( _Hero and Heroine_).

![45. Procol Harum](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-procolharum_hulton.jpg?w=980&q=75)

45\. Procol Harum

Hulton Archive, Getty Images

## 45\. Procol Harum

[Procol Harum](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/procol-harum/) arrived at a pivotal time, helping usher in proto-prog with the frilly baroque flair of their self-titled 1967 debut. But they’re rarely positioned among the genre’s other giants — probably because Gary Brooker’s soulful voice and the careful cadence of Keith Reid’s lyrics kept the band accessible, even at their most ambitious. But few bands created a sound so regal, so triumphant — especially when they roped in the orchestrations on classic tracks like “Grand Hotel” and “A Salty Dog.” “I don’t think Procol has ever fit into a particular pigeonhole, as we call them here, you know, in the filing cabinet,” Brooker told [Vintage Rock](https://vintagerock.com/the-gary-brooker-interview-2019/). “You don’t really know what to put them under. They come under ‘P’ — ‘Progressive?’ ‘Psychedelic?’ — and I say, ‘They come under ‘P,’ and ‘P’ is for ‘Procol.’”

![44. Steve Hillage](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-hillageyoutube.jpg?w=980&q=75)

44\. Steve Hillage

YouTube

## 44\. Steve Hillage

During the ‘70s, Steve Hillage became Canterbury scene royalty — both as a guitar wiz in other bands (including Gong and his lesser-known, shortly lived Khan) and as a solo artist always eager to experiment. His albums from this fertile period — particularly the trio of _Fish Rising_, the [Todd Rundgren](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/todd-rundgren/)-produced _L_ and _Motivation Radio_ — hold up to anything you can throw up in comparison, full of sublime space-rock guitar and balanced full-band arrangements. Like his onetime Gong bandmate Daevid Allen, he also showed a fanciful sense of humor, plastering a strange smile on signature excursions like “Solar Musick Suite” and “Light in the Sky.”

![43. Henry Cow](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-henrycowyoutube.jpg?w=980&q=75)

43\. Henry Cow

YouTube

## 43\. Henry Cow

In a sense, it’s unfair to label Henry Cow “prog” since their music pushed so viscerally against the confines of genre, particularly any form of commercial rock. The band, formed in 1968 by Cambridge students Fred Frith and Tim Hodgkinson, became the semiformal leaders of an experimental movement called Rock in Opposition (or RIO), which drew on contemporary classical and avant-garde more than anything you’d find on a Billboard chart. Across a handful of standard and collaborative LPs in the early to mid-‘70s, Henry Cow blurred the line beautifully between discordant and mellifluous, pairing conventional rock instruments with violin, clarinet, bassoon, xylophone and Farfisa organ. A small cluster of bands sprouted from this one seed, but none was more captivating than the Cow.

![42. Area](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-area.jpg?w=980&q=75)

42\. Area

YouTube

## 42\. Area

Cofounded by the inimitable frontman Demetrio Stratos, Area emerged from Milan in 1972 — two years after PFM’s origin in the same city. But their chaotic combination was wholly unique: jazz-fusion grooves led by fretless bass and synthesizers, free-jazz absurdity, experimental noise, sociopolitical concepts, Eastern melodies and Stratos’ octave-fluttering voice. The band’s first five albums — from 1973’s _Arbeit macht frei_ to _1978 Gli Dei Se Ne Vanno, Gli Arrabbiati Restano!_ — mark one of the hottest streaks in all of prog. But Stratos’ departure (and, soon after, his death) brought everything to a halt. “Being friends with him, it gave me the idea to write a song with the lyrics: ‘You are the master of the voice, teach me how to sing a song,’” PFM drummer Franz Di Cioccio told Hit Channel in 2015. A fitting tribute.

![41. Curved Air](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-curvedair_hulton.jpg?w=980&q=75)

41\. Curved Air

Hulton Archive, Getty Images

## 41\. Curved Air

Lineup shifts and a relatively short prime-era life span made Curved Air a tantalizing “What If?” Few prog bands were able to convincingly borrow from psychedelia, classical and hard rock — a blend showcased on their hit “Back Street Luv.” Violinist Darryl Way, keyboardist Francis Monkman and singer Sonja Kristina were the engine of their classic early LPs, including 1971’s _Second Album_ and the following year’s _Phantasmagoria_. A reconfigured Curved Air never reached the same heights, with one enormous exception: “Metamorphosis,” a 10-minute epic led by the stirring piano of briefly tenured multi-instrumentalist (and future [Roxy Music](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/roxy-music/) and U.K. member) Eddie Jobson.

![40. Focus](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-focusyoutube.jpg?w=980&q=75)

40\. Focus

YouTube

## 40\. Focus

“I don’t believe in the words ‘progressive rock,’” Focus’ Thijs van Leer told [_Prog_](https://www.loudersound.com/news/thijs-van-leer-lets-rip-into-the-state-of-todays-prog) in 2019. ”I think the only progressive rocker we ever had, who unfortunately died, was [Frank Zappa](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/frank-zappa/), because he combined modern classical music, which he composed himself, with rock.” Perhaps his definition is a bit too narrow: Focus, of course, created their own unique fusion of sounds, sprinkling classical, jazz-fusion and balls-out hard rock into their sonic buffet. All of those ingredients are present in their most famous tune, the 1971 hit “Hocus Pocus,” a surreal display of showboating that weaves in metallic riffs, yodeling, whistling, scatting, accordion, a lengthy drum solo and an absurdly high falsetto that most doctors would advise you not to sing along with. But the Dutch group were on fire through most of the ‘70s, particularly on the stretch from 1971’s _Focus II_ through 1974’s _Hamburger Concerto_.

![39. Goblin](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-goblinyoutube.jpg?w=980&q=75)

39\. Goblin

YouTube

## 39\. Goblin

Italy’s Goblin are revered in two fields of fandom that rarely overlap: prog die-hards and horror-soundtrack fiends. And they’ve managed to navigate both worlds with ease, dating back to the mid-‘70s, following a name change from Cherry Five. Their first major Goblin project proved crucial, crafting the creepy-crawly score to director Dario Argento’s 1975 classic _Profondo Rosso_ (or _Deep Red_). Their distinct style — melding Crimson-like heaviness, jazz-funk chops and gothic atmosphere — became their calling card throughout that decade and the next, as they teamed with filmmakers like George A. Romero ( _Martin_) and many others. And they became a go-to for Argento, working on several more of his projects, most notably on their respective 1977 masterpiece, _Suspiria_. The band’s non-soundtrack LPs never reached the same level of fame, but they’re equally worth investigating — start with the 1975 instrumental classic _Roller_, full of frenzied funk grooves and devilish organ atmospheres.

![38. Steve Hackett](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-hackett_iandickson.jpg?w=980&q=75)

38\. Steve Hackett

Ian Dickson, Getty Images

## 38\. Steve Hackett

All the Genesis guys have made compelling music on their own — just not always in the prog idiom. But [Steve Hackett](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/steve-hackett/) has consistently flown the flag, starting with his debut solo LP, 1975’s _Voyage of the Acolyte_, and continuing through his various records, one-off collaborations ( _Squackett_, a project with [Yes](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/yes/)’ [Chris Squire](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/chris-squire/)) and special tours (the Genesis Revisited series). He isn’t batting 1.000 quality-wise (let’s skip over the [GTR](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/gtr/) era). But he’s always fearless at the plate, willing to swing at just about any project fired his direction — from dabbling in multicultural sounds to recording with the Royal Philharmonic. Few artists, if any, have stayed prog — and, more importantly, stayed _interesting_ — for so long.

![37. Coheed and Cambria](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-candc_johnnylouisgetty_attachment-riot_fest_2021_must_see_bands_coheed_and_cambria.jpg?w=980&q=75)

37\. Coheed and Cambria

Johnny Louis, Getty Images

## 37\. Coheed and Cambria

Excluding their obvious imitators (and there are a few), no other band sounds like Coheed and Cambria. Like most of the relevant prog acts of the 21st century, their music is largely rooted in detuned, distorted riffs — but they’re just as likely to spark off a power-pop chorus, crank out some emo-metal guitar fireworks and settle into synth ambience. That combination was largely in place right out of the gate on 2002’s _The Second Stage Turbine Blade_, the first installment of Claudio Sanchez’s overarching conceptual narrative _The Amory Wars_. But their songwriting has only sharpened over the years — from the sugary sing-alongs (“A Favor House Atlantic”) to full-throttle epics (“No World for Tomorrow”).

![36. Hawkwind](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-hawkwind.jpg?w=980&q=75)

36\. Hawkwind

Hulton Archive, Getty Images

## 36\. Hawkwind

Though they’re rightly cited as the forefathers of space-rock, [Hawkwind](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/hawkwind/) didn’t fit easily into any one box. Over dozens of albums, including landmarks like 1971’s _In Search of Space_ and 1973’s double-live [_Space Ritual_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/hawkwind-space-ritual/), they’ve refined a snarling, psychedelic sound laced with synthesizers, electronics, heavy guitars, woodwinds and the out-there poetry of Robert Calvert. “With Hawkwind, I always considered them the working-man’s version of the [Pink Floyd](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/pink-floyd/),” saxophonist Nik Turner told [Something Else!](https://somethingelsereviews.com/2013/04/11/something-else-interview-nik-turner-co-founder-of-hawkwind/) “It was all psychedelic, with lots of strobe lights, and there were always drugs. It was a bit like the [Grateful Dead](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/the-grateful-dead/), really, in that people used to come to the gigs and have life-changing experiences.”

![Pictures Alliance, Getty Images](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-marillion_picturesalliance.jpg?w=980&q=75)

Pictures Alliance, Getty Images

## 35\. Marillion

Just like Genesis, one of their obvious and noted influences, [Marillion](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/marillion/) replaced one charismatic singer with another — and for many fans, it’s easier to think of each lineup as a different band altogether. From 1981 to 1988, Marillion were fronted by Fish, whose psychological lyrics and theatrical style positioned them as leaders of “neo-prog” — a movement best exemplified by their sleek debut, _Script for a Jester’s Tear_, and U.K. chart-topper [_Misplaced Childhood_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/marillion-misplaced-childhood/). But they managed to keep their momentum with new vocalist Steve Hogarth, who brought sensitivity and a wider physical range to the textured light-and-shade prog of post-Fish staples like 1989’s _Seasons End_ and 1994’s _Brave_.

![34. Eloy](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-eloy.jpg?w=980&q=75)

34\. Eloy

YouTube

## 34\. Eloy

Eloy were one of most consistent bands during prog’s ‘70s heyday, firing off one near-classic after another for close to a decade. The German band, led by guitarist and regular producer Frank Bornemann, were masters of space-rock mood, wringing out every ounce of drama on albums like 1977’s _Ocean_ and 1979’s _Silent Cries and Mighty Echoes_. (Bornemann himself accurately points to 1971’s _Inside_ as their true stylistic birth. “We were able now to create a mixture of pulsating rhythms and atmospheres,” he told [It’s Psychedelic Baby](https://www.psychedelicbabymag.com/2011/10/eloy-interview-with-frank-bornemann.html). “The sound of Eloy was born.”) Many casual fans have trouble digesting the frontman’s half-spoken vocal delivery and heavy accent — lucky for them, there are blissful instrumental sections in almost every song.

![33. Supertramp](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-supertramp.jpg?w=980&q=75)

33\. Supertramp

Hulton Archive, Getty Images

## 33\. Supertramp

“I don't even know what that means!” [Roger Hodgson](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/roger-hodgson/) told [Eclipsed](https://www.eclipsed.de/en/current/am-fruhstucksbufett-interview-roger-hodgson), reflecting on the “question of whether or not [Supertramp](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/supertramp/) were a progressive rock band.” Here’s where we consult the age-old rule: If you do prog enough of the time, you’re in the club. The band’s career arc is fascinating — starting off in a more generic art-rock territory on its first two LPs before finding a sweet spot between hookiness (“Dreamer”) and expansiveness (“School”) on 1974’s _Crime of the Century_, the first featuring Supertramp's classic quintet lineup. The band’s international breakthrough, 1979’s [_Breakfast in America_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/supertramp-breakfast-in-america/), tweaked the ratio more toward sleek, artfully crafted pop — a peak in craftsmanship, even if their most rigid fans pined for the old days. Supertramp are one of rock’s most underrated bands, and their “are they/aren’t they?” status only makes them underdogs on the prog side.

![32. Vangelis](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-vangelis.jpg?w=980&q=75)

32\. Vangelis

YouTube

## 32\. Vangelis

Greek composer Evangelos Odysseas Papathanassíou will be forever linked to six notes: the dramatic piano theme that opens “Chariots of Fire,” an unlikely No. 1 hit lifted from the 1981 film of the same name. But his solo catalog is all over the map stylistically, balancing moments of such windswept sweetness with journeys into nightmarish darkness. After leaving psych-prog band Aphrodite’s Child, the multi-instrumentalist worked largely on his own, overdubbing keyboard-heavy arrangements that balanced symphonic prog with electronica, classical and New Age “space music.”

![31. Nektar](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-nektar.jpg?w=980&q=75)

31\. Nektar

YouTube

## 31\. Nektar

Nektar were an unusual band in their early days: a bunch of Brits based in Hamburg, employing one (briefly two) full-time members to create trippy stage visuals. And nobody else sounded quite like their soulful spin on space rock, with singer-guitarist Roye Albrighton adding earthly grittiness and angst to their sci-fi narratives and cosmic keyboards. Various formations of Nektar carried the brand forward over the decades, building on a series of classic LPs from the early to mid-‘70s, including 1972’s _A Tab in the Ocean_ and 1973’s _Remember the Future_.

![30. Banco del Mutuo Soccorso](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-banco.jpg?w=980&q=75)

30\. Banco del Mutuo Soccorso

YouTube

## 30\. Banco del Mutuo Soccorso

For a multitude of reasons — among them technology, cultural trends and an overall explosion of creativity — many of the bands on this list thrived in the ‘70s. Italy’s Banco del Mutuo Soccorso were chief among them, releasing seven solid-to-classic records before a dramatic nosedive in quality the following decade. At their peak, they focused on capital-R Romantic symph-prog, carried by the operatic, exuberant vocals of Francesco Di Giacomo and the dual keyboards of brothers Vittorio and Gianni Nocenzi. While any Banco fan should soak in all of the band’s early material, their first three albums (1972’s _Banco del Mutuo Soccorso_ and _Darwin_, 1973’s _Io sono nato libero_) belong in the all-time trophy case.

![29. Tangerine Dream](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-tangerine-dream.jpg?w=980&q=75)

29\. Tangerine Dream

YouTube

## 29\. Tangerine Dream

“We’ve never ever created ‘electronic music!’” Edgar Froese told [The Quietus](https://thequietus.com/articles/03878-edgar-froese-tangerine-dream-interview) in 2010. “Of course, I love the guitar a lot, Motown stuff as well as modern progressive rock music.” That sentiment is key: [Tangerine Dream](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/tangerine-dream/) may be electronic pioneers, but they experimented with synths and sequencers through a prog lens. In fact, the German band started out in the mode of “Kosmiche musik” (“cosmic music”), an apt description of its trance-y early ‘70s drones. And they cleverly blended the organic and the synthetic throughout the decade, influencing a future generation of lesser copycats with the blissful instrumental textures of 1974’s _Phaedra_, 1975’s _Rubycon_ and 1978’s _Force Majeure_.

![28. Renaissance](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-renaissance-1.jpg?w=980&q=75)

28\. Renaissance

## 28\. Renaissance

“A lot of people call us a progressive rock band,” singer Annie Haslam told [Hit Channel](https://www.hit-channel.com/interview-annie-haslam-renaissance/138132) in 2018. “I say all the time that we are a symphonic rock band, because we are not that heavy.” True, [Renaissance](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/renaissance/) have always been on the lighter, more studious end of the prog spectrum — but they created genuinely symphonic sounds, either through the raw expressiveness of their playing (including John Tout’s classical-inspired piano and Haslam’s quivering, operatic voice) or by recording with actual orchestras (as they did on 1975’s [_Scheherazade and Other Stories_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/renaissance-scheherazade-and-other-stories/) and the 1976 concert LP _Live at Carnegie Hall_).

## 27\. Traffic

## 26\. Porcupine Tree

Steven Wilson has a complicated relationship with the term “prog” — while promoting his fifth solo LP, 2017’s _To the Bone_, he told [_Decibel_](https://www.decibelmagazine.com/2018/08/20/steven-wilson-prog/) that he “took great delight” in destroying his proggy image. But “prog” is pretty much the only accurate label for Porcupine Tree, his original project-turned-legit-band, which updated the genre for the alt-rock/metal age. Few bands of the era can touch the decade-long run from 1999’s _Stupid Dream_ to 2009’s _The Incident_.

## 25\. Soft Machine

[Soft Machine](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/soft-machine/) were basically the command center of the Canterbury scene: [Kevin Ayers](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/kevin-ayers/) and Gong’s Daevid Allen served brief stints in the lineup, and journeyman Robert Wyatt was a key figure during their early transition from psychedelia to freewheeling jazz-rock on 1970’s _Third_ and 1971’s _Fourth_. Every album kept the revolving door moving, including explosive playing from guitar god [Allan Holdsworth](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/allan-holdsworth/) on 1975’s _Bundles_. By the release of _Land of Cockayne_ six years later, not a single original member remained. That constant evolution results in a messy but fascinating catalog, each album a blurry Polaroid of a band in constant movement.

## 24\. The Moody Blues

“It was just a great time," John Lodge told [UCR](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/john-lodge-moody-blues-prog-rock/), looking back at the [Moody Blues](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/the-moody-blues/)’ late-‘60s emergence. "We were all sort of progressing our music in a way that was different to AM music. We were going somewhere different and for me, it was really interesting to listen to Yes and to see how far they had stretched their musical adaptation of their music and what they saw as rock 'n' roll.” The band had superficial similarities to Yes: the mellotrons, the vocal harmonies, the overall symphonic scale. But the Moodies always seemed to cruise down their own lane, taking a less bombastic and more pop-friendly approach than most of their prog contemporaries. Context is always important: Many of their definitive early albums (including the symphonic-rock fusion of 1967’s [_Days of Future Passed_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/moody-blues-days-of-future-passed-album/)) arrived well before canonical early masterpieces King Crimson’s [_In the Court of the Crimson King_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/king-crimson-crimson-king/). And even down the road, the group’s tunefulness make them unique.

## 23\. Ange

Lots of ‘70s prog bands were theatrical, using costumes and craziness to jazz up their live show. But none of them had the intensity of France’s Ange, the long-running symphonic act formed by the Decamps brothers, Christian (vocals, keyboards) and Francis (keyboards). The former’s outlandish vocals — conjuring a Shakespearian actor one second, a circus ringmaster the next — are easily their signature element, the glue connecting all of their six sturdy ‘70s LPs (including their 1974 masterpiece, _Au-dela du delire_). But their outrageousness has always felt genuinely human, using reverb-coated organs and expressive guitars to help stage their melodrama of the soul.

## 22\. Le Orme

This Venice group, fronted for most of its existence by angel-voiced bassist Aldo Tagliapietra, started out in the late ‘60s beat-psych scene — a far cry from the symph-prog splendor of their classic era. They briefly attempted an international breakthrough, landing Peter Hammill’s English lyrics for a revised version of 1973’s _Felona e Sorona_. But they’re mostly remembered as kings of their Romantic corner of Rock Progressivo Italiano — and one of the most consistent prog bands of any country. While newcomers should start with _Felona_, their spaciest and hookiest work, their nine-album period from 1971’s _Collage_ to 1980’s _Piccola rapsodia dell’ape_ is almost entirely next-level.

## 21\. Magma

You wouldn’t think any band would be nuts enough to trace Magma’s idiosyncratic footsteps. But an entire movement — Zeuhl — has sprung from the group’s weird brand of prog. It’s difficult to describe: operatic choirs, jazz-fusion grooves and vocals sung in an invented alien lexicon (Kobaiian) and set within a sort of science-fiction mythology. (“I think that Magma is not a prog rock group at all!" the band’s founder, leader and drummer told [Musoscribe](http://blog.musoscribe.com/index.php/2017/12/28/the-magma-mega-interview-part-three/). He might take issue with even being placed on this list.) Naturally, for all their imitators in this super niche sub-subgenre, no one ever outdid the thrill of Magma’s most enduring work, particularly their third LP, 1973’s _Mekanik Destruktiw Kommandoh_.

## 20\. Opeth

Mikael Akerfeldt is not only a prog innovator — he’s an unabashed fan and collector, schooling fans on buried treasures like Goblin, Carmen and Comus. “It’s really beautiful when you discover these types of bands,” the songwriter told [_Rolling Stone_](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/opeth-on-how-romantic-mindf-ks-obscure-prog-inspired-new-lp-249571/). “You can really tap into the local or the domestic scene at the time. The Italian scene is completely different from the U.S. scene, which is in turn completely different from the Scandinavian scene, etcetera.” He’s become a sort of prog professor — but he’s also built quite the curriculum with his own band, Sweden’s Opeth, who gradually evolved from dynamic, croon-to-growl death-metal (1995’s _Orchid_) to a more melodic style with nods to jazz-fusion, Eastern music, hard rock and symphonic prog. Many Opeth die-hards jumped off the bandwagon in the late '00s, as Akerfeldt grew bored of modern metal production and sought inspiration elsewhere. Their loss — the band’s catalog grows only more vibrant over time.

## 19\. Kansas

Mixing heartland boogie rock and symphonic complexity reads on paper like a ludicrous idea — and it often sounds that way, too. But that’s part of the charm with Topeka’s own Kansas, one of the few American prog bands to register even a blip on the Billboard charts. Led in their ‘70s prime by the enormous, AOR-friendly voice of Steve Walsh, the regal violin of Robby Steinhardt and the multi-instrumentalist chops of Kerry Livgren, the group entered the pop consciousness with the twisty rock staple “Carry On Wayward Son” and lighter-lit ballad “Dust in the Wind.” But hardcore prog fans still find plenty of nerdy thrills tucked away in the deep cuts, from the multipart 1975 epic “Magnum Opus” to the solo-stuffed 2020 barnburner “The Absence of Presence.”

## 18\. Premiata Forneria Marconi

Like Britain, Italy had their own big three in the ‘70s: Le Orme, Banco del Mutuo Soccorso and this long-surviving, long-titled band. Premiata Forneria Marconi originated from Milan in 1970, building an early repertoire of prog covers (including King Crimson and [Jethro Tull](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/jethro-tull/)) before crafting originals of equal intrigue and excitement. Their first three LPs — 1972’s _Storia di un minuto_ and _Per un amico_, 1974’s _L’isola di niente_ — are essentials in the canon: symphonic and memorably melodic, by turns heavy and jazzy, elevated into the stratosphere by Mauro Pagani’s violin and flute. Member turnover dulled that majesty later on, but there’s plenty to savor in every PFM era — including, on albums like 1975’s _Chocolate Kings_ — the divisive bleating-goat vocal style of onetime frontman Bernardo Lanzetti.

## 17\. Can

“When I founded Can, I didn’t think about a rock group,” Can keyboardist Irmin Schmidt told [_Prog_](https://www.loudersound.com/features/we-never-saw-ourselves-as-a-rock-group-the-prog-interview-with-cans-irmin-schmidt) in 2019. “I wanted to bring together jazz, rock, new music and ethnic experiences of different people and find out what happens. Whatever you want to call them, Can were among the most radical semi-mainstream bands of the 20th century, falling somewhere between psychedelia, funk and the truly avant-garde on masterpieces like 1971’s [_Tago Mago_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/can-tago-mago/) and 1973’s _Future Days_.

## 16\. Emerson, Lake & Palmer

They invented the prog supergroup, redefined the notion of classical rock and took onstage flamboyance and excess to comical new heights. Uniting in 1970, keyboardist [Keith Emerson](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/keith-emerson/) (from the [Nice](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/the-nice/)), singer-bassist [Greg Lake](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/greg-lake/) (King Crimson) and drummer [Carl Palmer](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/carl-palmer/) (Atomic Rooster) weren’t always the most compatible bandmates — the former two often sparred over the trio’s musical direction. But that tension made them fascinating, with Emerson’s outrageous Hammond and synth workouts bumping up against Lake’s riff- and chorus-driven rock. They were guilty of wankery on occasion — no argument there. But when these two clashing musical concepts coalesced (see: lengthy epics “Tarkus” and “Karn Evil 9”), the effect was magical.

## 15\. Mike Oldfield

## 14\. The Mars Volta

## 13\. Van der Graaf Generator

“I loved [Van der Graaf](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/van-der-graaf-generator/),” [Rush](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/rush/)’s [Geddy Lee](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/geddy-lee/) told [_Rolling Stone_](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/rush-geddy-lee-bass-book-interview-767961/) in 2018, noting his catalog of that band’s ‘70s vinyl. “They had a dark and sort of brooding sound that I really liked at the time.” But not everyone has that man’s elite taste — and even fewer can handle the rabid intensity and foaming-at-the-mouth theatricality of Peter Hammill’s songs, best displayed on masterpieces like 1971’s _Pawn Hearts_ and 1975’s _Godbluff_. “The idea of being a super-successful band was anathema to us from the outset,” the songwriter told [_The Guardian_](https://www.theguardian.com/music/2016/oct/14/van-der-graaf-generator-peter-hammill-interview-do-not-disturb) in 2016. “We always wanted to be twittering around with chaotic and raucous stuff.” They did indeed, bridging the gap between symph-prog and punk, two genres briefly locked in a struggle for supremacy.

## 12\. Caravan

Four Canterbury mainstays jump-started Caravan in 1968, releasing their psych-heavy (and often overlooked) debut LP that same year. ## 11\. Gong

Daevid Allen’s first major career move was cofounding Soft Machine, a band that later flourished as jazzy figureheads of the Canterbury scene. But after the Australian guitarist was denied reentry into the U.K. due to an expired visa, he stuck around Paris and reconfigured his entire life and musical vision, forming the whimsical space-rock outfit Gong. The band evolved considerably over the years — following Allen’s temporary exit in the mid-‘70s, they moved completely into a fusion-y, percussion-heavy sound led by Pierre Moerlen. But they’ll remain forever known for “Radio Gnome Invisible,” an earlier trilogy ( _Flying Teapot_, _Angel’s Egg_, _You_) balancing Allen’s fantasy lyrics and warped pop melodies, the cosmic “space whispers” of Gilli Smyth, Steve Hillage’s psychedelic guitar solos and the exotic woodwinds of Didier Malherbe.

## 10\. Tool

The raggedness and relative simplicity of [Tool](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/tool/)’s debut EP, 1992’s _Opiate_, only illustrates the vastness of their transformation. Their back-to-back masterpieces, _AEnima_ and _Lateralus_, cemented the quartet as their generation’s most influential heavy band, drawing on [_Red_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/king-crimson-red/)-era Crimson acid-trip psychedelia more than anything in the alt-metal realm. The instrumentalists — particularly drummer Danny Carey, who married the precise virtuosity of [Neil Peart](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/neil-peart/) and the bombast of Billy Cobham — ensured their lofty prog status with time signatures you need a math degree to decode. And frontman Maynard James Keenan brought in the humanity, singing about philosophical and existential concepts with a rare mix of dark humor and heart.

## 9\. Camel

“As a young musician … three \[guitarists\] really inspired me,” Marillion’s Steve Rothery [said](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tn7E1LdC0wU) onstage at the 2014 Prog Awards. “ [David Gilmour](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/david-gilmour/) of Pink Floyd, my good friend Steve Hackett of Genesis and \[Andy Latimer\], whose beautiful, lyrical and emotional style of playing was a constant source of inspiration.” It’s a perfect summation of Latimer’s gifts — he’s one of the most expressive guitarists in all of rock, even if he’s rarely mentioned in the same breath as the others above. And that tasteful approach applies to everyone who passed though the Camel ranks — particularly the quartet lineup from the early ‘70s, who churned out classic LP after classic LP. The band would have made this list even if it had stopped after 1976’s _Moonmadness_, the last of Camel's inarguable masterpieces. But they persevered through the neon decade and beyond, with Latimer steering the ship — always with class, never with show-off flash.

## 8\. Jethro Tull

“It’s something rock, and whatever that ‘something’ is, I still like the original term that comes from 1969: progressive rock,” [Ian Anderson](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/ian-anderson/) told [Something Else!](https://somethingelsereviews.com/2013/06/19/something-else-interview-ian-anderson-of-jethro-tull/) in 2013. “But that was with a small ‘p’ and a small ‘r.’ Prog rock, on the other hand, has different connotations — of grandeur and pomposity.” Those are the very qualities Anderson spoofed (and, to some extent, celebrated) on Jethro Tull’s overstuffed 1972 masterpiece, [_Thick as a Brick_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/jethro-tull-thick-as-a-brick/). But a less manic, more graceful progginess holds together their entire catalog, including other ‘70s staples like 1971’s [_Aqualung_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/jethro-tull-aqualung/) and the folk-rock trilogy of _Songs From the Wood_, [_Heavy Horses_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/jethro-tull-heavy-horses/) and [_Stormwatch_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/jethro-tull-stormwatch/). Many prog bands were determined to flaunt their chops above all else — and even if Tull could outplay just about anybody (see all of _A Passion Play_, for example), they never sacrificed melody or self-awareness.

## 7\. Gentle Giant

“People say ‘progressive,’ but I think we were more than a rock band than whatever ‘progressive’ meant — a rock band who did things in a quirky way,” singer Derek Shulman told [UCR](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/gentle-giant-derek-shulman-interview/). “But certainly R&B and groove and soul were part of the band, and we never got away from that, even though people said we were Old English and ‘medieval’ and jazz or whatever.” And that’s an overlooked aspect of the [Gentle Giant](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/gentle-giant/) aesthetic: Most of their weirdest moves (the intricate vocal counterpoint, the instrument-hopping, the complex chord progressions) were anchored in groove and melody. The key was continual surprise — a philosophy that fueled 11 studio albums in one decade, including masterpieces like 1972’s [_Octopus_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/gentle-giant-octopus/) and 1975’s [_Free Hand_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/gentle-giant-free-hand/). “We didn't want to have people sit in their hands and know what's coming next, or have pretentious keyboard parts that tried to be like a symphony orchestra,” Shulman added. “We wanted to keep people on their feet.”

## 6\. Rush

“‘For us it was so authentic, so real, so sincere, that we were getting better and learning how to play these songs,” Rush’s Neil Peart told [_Rolling Stone_](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/rush-neil-peart-podcast-tribute-941028/) in 2015, looking back at the band’s evolution during the golden age of prog pretension. That sense of purity was always key to the Canadian power-trio — no matter the era, Rush never played a false note. It also fueled their longevity: They survived through punk and new wave and synth-pop and grunge, absorbing stylistic elements here and there to keep their music fresh. When Geddy Lee started playing synthesizers in the ‘80s, he committed to the instrument as a compositional tool — never a gimmick. And when [Alex Lifeson](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/alex-lifeson/)’s guitars got heavier in the ‘90s, it felt like an organic reaction to the move before that. Rush recorded essential albums in every era, from their pure-prog summit of the late ‘70s ( _Hemispheres_) to their sleeker sounds in the following decade ( [_Moving Pictures_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/rush-moving-pictures-album/)) to the late-career triumph of [_Clockwork Angels_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/rush-clockwork-angels-album-review/). All of it was, indeed, “so real.” And most of it so very good.

## 5\. Frank Zappa

“I wouldn’t describe myself as ‘progressive rock,’ Frank Zappa told [MTV](https://youtu.be/Eln3J6BxWN0?t=442) in 1984. “In fact a lot of the time it’s not rock 'n' roll at all — it just happens to be consumed by rock 'n' roll audiences.” He had a point: Zappa’s sprawling, intimidating catalog winds through classical, Synclavier experiments, avant-garde dissonance, sound manipulation, jazz-fusion, R&B, psychedelia, sonic satire — the only real connective tissue is the composer’s unconventional approach to harmony and rhythm. But so much of his most beloved work happens to be prog-rock-adjacent, like the dizzying instrumental passages of 1969’s [_Hot Rats_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/frank-zappa-hot-rats/) and 1974’s _One Size Fits All_.

## 4\. Pink Floyd

A lack of technical skill can often be a boon: [Pink Floyd](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/pink-floyd/) were far from virtuosos, but they played with more raw emotion than almost anyone else in the prog arena — helping their spacey, lyrically biting songs transcend shelf lives altogether. A lot of fans even question their place in the genre, probably because the band never relied on technique to captivate an audience. Then again, a lot of fans are dumb. Ambition and artfulness tie together the whole Floyd catalog — from their late-‘60s psych-rock experiments with original leader [Syd Barrett](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/syd-barrett/) ( [_The Piper at the Gates of Dawn_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/pink-floyd-debut-the-piper-at-the-gates-of-dawn-turns-45/)) through their concept-focused, lavishly produced ‘70s peak ( [_The Dark Side of the Moon_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/pink-floyd-dark-side-of-the-moon/), [_Wish You Were Here_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/pink-floyd-wish-you-were-here/)).

Redferns, Getty Images

## 3\. Yes

[Yes](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/yes/) recorded both the greatest progressive rock song (“Close to the Edge”) and album ( [_Close to the Edge_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/yes-close-to-the-edge-turns-40/)) — hard for anyone to argue with a top three pick. And the rest of their resume is pretty impressive: A handful of the genre’s most beloved players ( [Steve Howe](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/steve-howe/), Rick Wakeman, [Bill Bruford](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/bill-bruford/), Chris Squire) have passed through their ranks, and almost no one can top their longevity (there have been few lulls in activity between 1969’s [_Yes_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/yes-debut-album/) and 2021’s [_The Quest_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/yes-the-quest-album/)). Sure, their most influential work ( [_The Yes Album_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/the-yes-album/), [_Fragile_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/yes-fragile-album/), [_Relayer_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/yes-relayer/)) arrived during the early and mid-‘70s. But few prog acts were able to survive such soap-opera levels of member turnover, let alone decades into their career. Even fewer could reinvent themselves through new wave ( [_Drama_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/yes-drama-album/)) and pop ( [_90125_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/yes-90125/)). Yes, to borrow an early song title, were built for “Survival.”

![2. Genesis](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-genesis.jpg?w=980&q=75)

2\. Genesis

Dennis Stone, Getty Images

## 2\. Genesis

The OG prog bands faced a tough choice in the ‘80s: evolve or go extinct. Some pulled it off: Yes (temporarily) with _90125_, King Crimson with [_Discipline_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/king-crimson-discipline-album/). But no one did it more organically than Genesis, who maintained their integrity while blowing up with some of the decade’s savviest stadium-sized pop. A lot of prog fans get all pompous when it comes to the [Phil Collins](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/phil-collins/) era, snubbing their noses at albums like [_Abacab_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/genesis-abacab-album/) and [_Invisible Touch_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/genesis-invisible-touch/). There are probably deeper reasons for that elitism — and we don’t have the space here to unpack them. But Genesis survived because those songs were as solid as oak trees: melodic, quirky, soulful, still dense with Tony Banks’ unorthodox chord changes. Meanwhile, the catalog of the ‘70s lineup with [Peter Gabriel](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/peter-gabriel/) — including the symphonic perfection of [_Foxtrot_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/genesis-foxtrot/) and [_Selling England by the Pound_](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/genesis-selling-england-by-the-pound/) — needs no defending among prog-heads.

![1. King Crimson](https://townsquare.media/site/295/files/2021/08/attachment-gettyimages-555277205.jpg?w=980&q=75)

1\. King Crimson

Rob Verhorst, Getty Images

## 1\. King Crimson

It’s almost impossible to rank prog’s Holy Trinity — they feel like one inseparable organism, inspiring worship and influencing basically everyone who followed their lead. The ultimate tiebreakers have to be longevity and consistency: King Crimson were there at the very beginning of the prog boom with 1969’s _In the Court of the Crimson King_, and (barring a few breaks and one major ‘70s hiatus) they really never went away, with [Robert Fripp](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/robert-fripp/) continuously reinventing the band in various configurations: the new wave-leaning ‘80s quartet, the raucous “double-trio” edition in the ‘90s, the assorted “projeKct” offshoots, the expansive triple-drummer outfit from the '10s. While many prog bands are content to coast on their legacy, recycling old sounds and sputtering when they attempt new ideas, King Crimson have reveled in the unknown — always keen to shine their flashlights in the dark.
